trigger_phrases: What are the risk tiers under the EU AI Act?
How does the EU AI Act classify AI systems by risk level?
unacceptable risk high risk limited risk minimal risk EU AI Act
canonical_context: The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) has no single list of four risk categories. "Unacceptable, high, limited and minimal risk" is a common summary of four separate parts of the Regulation; of those labels, only "high-risk" is the Regulation's own term. (1) Unacceptable risk: Article 5, "Prohibited AI practices" (Chapter II), practices banned outright, for example subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques (Article 5(1)(a)) and social scoring (Article 5(1)(c)). (2) High risk: Article 6, "Classification rules for high-risk AI systems": AI that is a safety component of, or itself, a product under the legislation in Annex I that needs third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)), or AI used in the areas listed in Annex III (Article 6(2)). High-risk systems must meet the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency to deployers, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity) and undergo conformity assessment (Article 43). Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is not high-risk if it poses no significant risk of harm, for example because it performs a narrow procedural task. (3) Limited risk: Article 50, "Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems": people must be told they are interacting with an AI system (Article 50(1)), synthetic audio, image, video or text must be marked as artificially generated (Article 50(2)), and deep fakes must be disclosed (Article 50(4)). (4) Minimal risk: all other AI systems, with no obligations tied to a risk class; Article 95 encourages voluntary codes of conduct, and the AI literacy duty in Article 4 applies to all providers and deployers.

trigger_phrases: What obligations apply to general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act?
How does the EU AI Act regulate foundation models?
EU AI Act ChatGPT GPT-4 generative AI regulation
canonical_context: The EU AI Act's articles don't use the term "generative AI", but its recitals do: recital 99 calls large generative AI models a typical example of a general-purpose AI model (see also recital 105). The model behind a chatbot like ChatGPT is a "general-purpose AI model" (Article 3(63)), regulated in Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56); the chatbot built on it is an AI system, a "general-purpose AI system" (Article 3(66)). Every provider of a general-purpose AI model must (Article 53(1)): (a) draw up and keep up to date technical documentation of the model, to provide on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities; (b) draw up, keep up to date and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate the model; (c) put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, including identifying and complying with rights reservations under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790; (d) draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training, using the AI Office's template. A model is a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities or the Commission designates it (Article 51(1)); high-impact capabilities are presumed when the cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations (Article 51(2)). Providers of those models must also (Article 55(1)): (a) perform model evaluation, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing; (b) assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level; (c) keep track of, document and report serious incidents and possible corrective measures without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, national competent authorities; (d) ensure adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. The AI system itself also carries transparency duties under Article 50: providers must make sure people are told they are interacting with an AI system (Article 50(1)), and providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark the outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)).

trigger_phrases: Are open-source AI models exempt from the EU AI Act?
EU AI Act open source licence exemption
canonical_context: The EU AI Act has three separate open-source rules, not one exemption. (1) AI systems, Article 2(12): the Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 (prohibited practices) or Article 50 (transparency obligations). (2) General-purpose AI models, Articles 53(2) and 54(6): a provider whose model is released under a free and open-source licence that allows access, usage, modification and distribution, and whose parameters, including the weights, the model architecture information and the model usage information are publicly available, is exempt from the technical-documentation duty (Article 53(1)(a)), the duty to inform downstream providers (Article 53(1)(b)) and the duty to appoint an authorised representative (Article 54). The provider must still put in place a copyright policy (Article 53(1)(c)) and publish the training-content summary (Article 53(1)(d)). These exceptions do not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk. (3) The AI value chain, Article 25(4): third parties that make tools, services, processes or components other than general-purpose AI models available to the public under a free and open-source licence don't have to sign the written agreement that suppliers to high-risk AI providers otherwise need; recital 89 encourages them to use documentation practices such as model cards and data sheets. Recital 103 adds that AI components provided against a price or otherwise monetised don't benefit from the open-source exceptions.

trigger_phrases: What categories make up the Govern function in NIST AI RMF 1.0?
What must organisations put in place under the AI RMF Govern function?
NIST AI RMF Govern function categories GOVERN 1 to GOVERN 6
canonical_context: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0), Table 1, defines six categories under the GOVERN function. GOVERN 1: Policies, processes, procedures, and practices across the organization related to the mapping, measuring, and managing of AI risks are in place, transparent, and implemented effectively. GOVERN 2: Accountability structures are in place so that the appropriate teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and trained for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks. GOVERN 3: Workforce diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility processes are prioritized in the mapping, measuring, and managing of AI risks throughout the lifecycle. GOVERN 4: Organizational teams are committed to a culture that considers and communicates AI risk. GOVERN 5: Processes are in place for robust engagement with relevant AI actors. GOVERN 6: Policies and procedures are in place to address AI risks and benefits arising from third-party software and data and other supply chain issues.

trigger_phrases: What is the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications?
OWASP top ten large language model risks
OWASP Top 10 risks for generative AI and LLM applications
Which vulnerabilities does OWASP list for LLM apps?
canonical_context: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 lists: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection - user or external input alters the model's behaviour or output in unintended ways, even when the input is not human-visible; RAG and fine-tuning do not fully prevent it. LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure - the model or application exposes personal data, credentials, confidential business data or proprietary details through its output. LLM03:2025 Supply Chain - third-party models, training data, fine-tuning adapters and deployment platforms can be tampered with or poisoned, compromising integrity. LLM04:2025 Data and Model Poisoning - pre-training, fine-tuning or embedding data is manipulated to introduce vulnerabilities, backdoors or biases; an integrity attack. LLM05:2025 Improper Output Handling - model output is passed downstream without sufficient validation or sanitisation, enabling XSS, CSRF, SSRF, privilege escalation or remote code execution. LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency - the system is granted more functionality, permissions or autonomy than needed, so unexpected or manipulated model output can trigger damaging actions. LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage - system prompts contain sensitive information (credentials, connection strings, roles and permissions) that can be extracted; the system prompt must not be treated as a secret or a security control. LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses - weaknesses in how vectors and embeddings are generated, stored or retrieved in RAG systems are exploited to inject content, manipulate output or access sensitive information. LLM09:2025 Misinformation - the model produces false or misleading information that appears credible, chiefly through hallucination, leading to security, reputational and legal harm. LLM10:2025 Unbounded Consumption - the application allows excessive and uncontrolled inference, enabling denial of service, financial loss (denial of wallet) or model theft by cloning.

trigger_phrases: What are the data protection principles in Article 5 of the GDPR?
Which principles relating to processing of personal data does GDPR set out?
GDPR lawfulness fairness transparency purpose limitation data minimisation principles
canonical_context: GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) Article 5, 'Principles relating to processing of personal data'. Article 5(1): personal data shall be (a) processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject ('lawfulness, fairness and transparency'); (b) collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes ('purpose limitation'); (c) adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed ('data minimisation'); (d) accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date ('accuracy'); (e) kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed ('storage limitation'); (f) processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures ('integrity and confidentiality'). Article 5(2): the controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, paragraph 1 ('accountability').

trigger_phrases: ISO 27001 mandatory documents and records
Which documents are mandatory for ISO 27001 certification audits?
What must an organisation document to be certified against ISO 27001?
canonical_context: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (third edition, 2022-10) contains no single list of mandatory documents; its clauses require documented information in these places: 4.3 the ISMS scope; 5.2 the information security policy; 6.1.2 the information security risk assessment process; 6.1.3 the risk treatment process, including the Statement of Applicability (6.1.3 d) and the risk treatment plan (6.1.3 e); 6.2 the information security objectives; 7.2 evidence of competence; 7.5.1 b) any further documented information the organization determines is necessary for ISMS effectiveness; 8.1 documented information to the extent needed for confidence that processes are carried out as planned; 8.2 the results of information security risk assessments; 8.3 the results of risk treatment; 9.1 evidence of monitoring and measurement results; 9.2.2 evidence of the internal audit programme and audit results; 9.3.3 evidence of management review results; 10.2 evidence of nonconformities, actions taken and the results of corrective action.
